title: A near-complete genome assembly of Anomia chinensis provides insights into bivalve phylogenomic evolution and mitochondrial UAA stop-to-Tyr codon reassignment in metazoans
abstract: Abstract Background The genetic code is evolutionarily conserved but can undergo lineage-specific alterations. Although mitochondrial UAA stop-to-Tyr codon reassignment has evolved independently in several metazoan lineages, its molecular basis remains poorly understood. As more species are sequenced, an increasing number of UAA stop-to-Tyr codon reassignments are being reported in new metazoan lineages, providing an important opportunity to integrate these cases and explore the molecular basis and evolutionary history of this reassignment. Results We generated a near-complete genome assembly of the cementing bivalve Anomia chinensis , a member of the understudied bivalve superfamily Anomioidea (Bivalvia, Mollusca), comprising 572.90 Mb with a contig N50 of 79.37 Mb and 7 chromosomes. A genome-based phylogeny reconstructed from the major lineages of Pteriomorphia supported that Pectinida is not monophyletic. We also reconstructed the bivalve ancestral linkage groups (BiLGs, n = 20) and performed macrosynteny analysis, which revealed that, within Pteriomorphia, cementing bivalves in the intertidal zone exhibited significantly lower conservation of ancestral karyotypes compared to other groups. Furthermore, we presented the first evidence of mitochondrial UAA stop-to-Tyr codon reassignment in bivalves. We further revealed the genetic basis underlying this reassignment in metazoan mitochondrial genomes, which generally requires the co-evolution of mtRF1a and tRNAs. Conclusions In this study, we provided essential genomic resources for A. chinensis and reconstructed the BiLGs of bivalves, advancing our understanding of bivalve phylogeny and chromosomal macrosynteny evolution. Importantly, the parallel mutations identified in mtRF1a and tRNA Tyr GUA in both hemichordates and mollusks may offer valuable insights into genetic code reprogramming of mitochondria in metazoans, and potentially across a broader range of cellular life.

title: Mesenchymal stem cell-derived exosomes alleviate renal interstitial fibrosis via pVHL-mediated HIF-1α ubiquitination and degradation
abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a global health burden that frequently progresses to renal interstitial fibrosis. Mesenchymal stem cell–derived exosomes (MSC-Ex) have shown therapeutic potential in kidney repair, yet their role in hypoxia-driven fibrosis remains undefined. We tested whether human umbilical cord MSC exosomes (hucMSC-Ex) attenuate fibrosis by delivering von Hippel-Lindau tumor suppressor protein (pVHL) to destabilize hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α). Hypoxia combined with mechanical stress increased nuclear HIF-1α levels in UUO tubules and triggered fibrosis. HucMSC-Ex markedly reduced renal collagen and α-SMA. Mechanistically, hucMSC-Ex were enriched in pVHL and increased pVHL abundance in recipient renal cells, promoting HIF-1α ubiquitination and proteasome-dependent degradation. HucMSC-Ex alleviate renal interstitial fibrosis by delivering pVHL to facilitate HIF-1α ubiquitination and degradation, thereby providing a cell-free anti-fibrotic strategy.

title: The brilliant future of non-traditional model organisms in biology
Accurate calling of low-frequency somatic mutations by sample-specific modeling of error rates
abstract: Abstract Calling rare somatic variants from NGS data is more challenging than calling inherited variants, especially if the somatic variant is only present in a small fraction of the cells in the sequenced biopsy. In this case, having a good estimate of the error rate of a specific base in a particular read becomes essential. In paired-end sequencing, where some DNA fragments are shorter than twice the read length, the overlapping regions of the read pairs are an ideal resource for training models to discern context-dependent base error rates, as any discordant bases in the overlaps must be caused by a sequencing error or an alignment error. We have created a new tool named BBQ (an acronym for Better Base Quality) that uses overlapping reads to estimate the error rate conditional on the mutation type, sequence context, and base quality. We also estimate how much the error rate of concordant bases in overlapping reads is decreased compared to bases in non-overlapping reads. Results show that overlapping reads can remove sequencing errors induced by DNA damage and that the increased quality of overlapping reads differs between samples and mutation types, reflecting different damage patterns between samples. We use the error models to call rare somatic variants. Sequencing data from a testis biopsy and a cell-free DNA sample serve as a proof-of-concept for rare germ cell mutation calling and for detecting rare cancer mutations. We find that using the sample-specific error models of BBQ allows us to call rare somatic variants with fewer false positives than existing tools such as Mutect2 and Strelka2.

title: The SH3b cell wall–binding domain of SpM23_B peptidoglycan hydrolase has antimicrobial activity
abstract: Bacterial peptidoglycan hydrolases (PGHs) are enzymes that degrade the peptidoglycan layer of bacterial cell walls and are essential for cell wall remodeling during growth, division, and cell wall turnover. PGHs commonly comprise an enzymatically active domain (EAD) and a cell wall–binding domain (CBD). Src Homology 3b (SH3b) domains are widely recognized as bacterial surface-targeting modules that enhance the activity and specificity of PGHs. However, their potential antimicrobial functions independent of the catalytic domain remain largely unexplored. Here, we investigated the antimicrobial properties of CBD_Sp_B, an SH3b domain derived from the SpM23_B PGH of Staphylococcus pettenkoferi . CBD_Sp_B exhibited potent bactericidal activity against all tested bacterial strains and, unexpectedly, also showed antifungal activity against multiple Candida species, including the WHO critical-priority pathogen Candida auris . Electron microscopy revealed pronounced ultrastructural alterations in both bacterial and fungal cells following treatment. SYTOX Green assays showed no significant membrane permeabilization, whereas DiSC 3 (5) measurements demonstrated a loss of bacterial membrane potential, indicating membrane depolarization as a component of its antimicrobial activity. Further analysis identified the C-terminal region of CBD_Sp_B as a key determinant of its antimicrobial function. However, its activity was strongly dependent on ionic strength and was abolished at NaCl concentrations ≥ 25 mM, limiting applications under physiological conditions. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized antimicrobial function of an SH3b domain, extending its biological role beyond bacterial cell-wall binding. The broad-spectrum bactericidal and antifungal activity of CBD_Sp_B highlights its potential as a novel antimicrobial scaffold, particularly for topical and non-clinical applications under low-ionic-strength conditions, while also providing a basis for engineering salt-tolerant derivatives.

title: Revealing a sustained increase in relative avian forelimb length through the Mesozoic
abstract: The evolution of avian flight is characterised by a gradual accumulation of various morphologies through time—yet an explicit temporal trend in wing length remains elusive. This is despite an expectation of increasing forelimbs leading to birds as seen in the fossil record and a clear theoretical expectation for an increase in wing length through time as a consequence of selection for improved flight performance from the earliest birds to the effective fliers we see today. Using Bayesian phylogenetic comparative methods across multiple phylogenies, we test for temporal trends in relative total forelimb length and individual forelimb bones through theropod evolution, whilst accounting for allometric relationships and assessing heterogeneity in the rates of evolution. We provide the first explicit evidence of a long-term trend towards increasing forelimb length in Mesozoic birds occurring independently of allometry-associated elongation and explain prior findings of heterogeneous rates in the evolution of the avialan forelimb bones. The use of methods which simultaneously account for relationships between traits and multiple hypotheses of their shared histories allows us to better understand the tempo and mode of transitions in locomotion—this is vital in understanding how flight evolved in early birds and how the elongation of the forelimbs played a part in their ultimate domination of the skies.

title: Quantifying effects of inattention on serial dependence in numerosity and orientation judgments using a Bayesian integration approach
abstract: Abstract Background Our perceptual judgments are influenced by recent experience. In three experiments, we examined how such serial dependence in numerosity and orientation judgments is influenced by attention. Participants estimated numerosity in dot clouds (Experiment 1) or the orientation of Gabor patches (Experiment 2: high contrast, Experiment 3: low contrast). These tasks were paired with an attention-demanding central task to modulate attention in a dual-task design. Results We found stronger serial dependence under divided attention across all experiments. Furthermore, we employed an ensemble of Bayesian models to disentangle the influence of attention, sensory evidence, and prior responses in numerosity and orientation judgments. Our six models differed in which of the three components of prior experience – average sensory evidence, prior sensory evidence and prior response – were included and how they expressed the influence of history on perceptual judgments. We found that all three factors influence perceptual judgments with attractive effects for prior responses and average sensory evidence, but a repulsive effect for prior sensory evidence. Importantly, the strength of the influence on individual components depended on the nature of the task (numerosity or orientation judgment), the quality of sensory evidence, and availability of attention. Conclusions Our findings suggest that perceptual decisions arise from a context-specific integration of prior experiences. This means that the magnitude and even the sign of serial dependence, whether it is overall attractive or repulsive, reflect specific combinations of factors (task, quality of evidence, attention, etc.) and highlight the importance of computational modeling for disentangling the individual effects.

title: A responsivity theory of call timing patterns in bat echolocation
abstract: Abstract Background The temporal patterning of bat echolocation is extensively characterised, but a general mathematical account linking call timing to acoustic propagation, relative motion, and behaviourally selected information remains incomplete. Results We present the responsivity framework, which represents each call event as a delayed active-sensing cycle comprising an acoustic acquisition interval and a subsequent behavioural interval. Their proportional relation is described by the responsivity coefficient, $$k_r$$ k r , connecting call timing to effective anchor distance, relative velocity, call duration, and the selected echo window. Analytical derivation, call-by-call simulation, internal validation, and comparison with field recordings show how the framework generates hyperbolic call-rate–distance relationships, shifts approach timing with echo-window selection, and places the terminal buzz at the near-target limit of the same timing process. Responsivity and kinematics have separable terminal effects: $$k_r$$ k r constrains terminal update density and attainable call rate, whereas closing velocity determines the time available within the terminal region. A buzz-readiness state precedes the complete expression of buzz, and transient sonar strobe groups emerge under multi-target anchor allocation without an explicit grouping rule. Field recordings show broad correspondence with simulations in the organisation of movement, call timing and call duration, and illustrate conditional evaluation of acquisition-window and anchor assumptions. Conclusions Responsivity theory provides a process-based descriptor of echolocation timing and a diagnostic framework for hypothesis generation and empirical testing. The framework identifies the measurements needed to test how selected acoustic information governs subsequent call timing.

title: Harnessing variation in Drosophila melanogaster reveals different routes to increased infection susceptibility over age and sex-dependent association with lifespan
abstract: Abstract Background It is widely accepted that susceptibility to infection increases with age, usually attributed to immune system dysregulation. However, factors beyond decreased resistance mechanisms may increase susceptibility, such as changes to physiological or metabolic processes determining overall tolerance, and this may differ between individuals. We hypothesised that age-related increases in susceptibility reflect changes in both immune system function and disease tolerance, with their relative importance varying by population and sex. Results We assessed age-related susceptibility to bacterial pathogens in an outbred Drosophila melanogaster population and 22 isolines. We leveraged this variation to investigate age-related infection susceptibility and lifespan and to estimate frequencies of declines in resistance or tolerance mechanisms. Susceptibility increased early in life and was widespread across infections and populations. Despite strong correlation between the sexes in baseline susceptibility and its decrease over age, susceptibility at old age did not correlate. Increased susceptibility was associated with impaired resistance ( bona fide immunosenescence), but more frequently with reduced tolerance, which could be detected early in life, and remained low. We find susceptibility at old age predicts lifespan in males only. Conclusions Increased infection susceptibility is an early-arising ageing phenotype occurring in both sexes and driving male mortality. Infection susceptibility followed a power-law (Weibull) rather than the exponential (Gompertz) pattern typical of mortality, with each doubling of age approximately doubling susceptibility. We argue that the term “immunosenescence” should be limited to dysregulation of resistance mechanisms, and consideration of population variation, sex, and ageing of non-immune functions is critical to fully understand age-related loss of pathogen control.
